Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they produce different histories.

## `git merge`

Creates a new commit that ties the two histories together.

```
main:    A---B---C---M
                  /
feature:  D---E---
```

- History is preserved exactly as it happened
- The merge commit records that a branch existed and when it was integrated
- Non-destructive — existing commits are untouched
- Fast-forwards instead of creating `M` when the target hasn't diverged

## `git rebase`

Replays your commits on top of the new base, one at a time.

```
main:    A---B---C---D'---E'
```

- Linear history, no merge commit
- `D'` and `E'` are **new commits** with different SHAs — the originals are discarded
- Conflicts are resolved per-commit, so you may hit the same conflict repeatedly (`git rerere` helps)
- Rewrites history, so pushing a rebased branch needs `--force-with-lease`

## Which to use

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch with new `main` | rebase |
| Merging a finished feature into `main` | merge (often `--no-ff`) |
| Branch is shared / already pushed and others pulled it | merge |
| Cleaning up messy WIP commits before review | `rebase -i` |

**The golden rule:** never rebase commits that exist outside your repository. If someone else has pulled the branch, rebasing rewrites shared history and their next pull becomes a mess.

## Practical middle ground

Many teams rebase locally to keep the branch current, then merge into `main` with a merge commit — you get readable linear feature history *and* a clear record of when each feature landed. GitHub's "Rebase and merge" and "Squash and merge" buttons are variations on the same idea.

A related option worth knowing: `git pull --rebase` (or `git config pull.rebase true`) avoids the noisy "Merge branch 'main' of origin..." commits that plague default `git pull`.

Both integrate changes from one branch into another. The difference is what they do to history.

## `git merge`

Creates a new **merge commit** with two parents, tying the branches together. Existing commits are never altered.

```
       A---B---C  feature
      /         \
 D---E---F---G---H  main      (H = merge commit)
```

- History is a faithful record of what actually happened, branch shape and all.
- Non-destructive — safe on branches other people have pulled.
- Log can get noisy: lots of "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commits, and `git log` interleaves parallel work.

## `git rebase`

Replays your commits on top of the new base, one at a time. Each replayed commit is a **new commit with a new SHA** — the originals are discarded (well, orphaned).

```
before:  A---B---C  feature
        /
   D---E---F---G  main

after:                A'--B'--C'  feature
                     /
   D---E---F---G  main
```

- History becomes linear and easy to read; `git bisect` and `git log` behave nicely.
- Rewrites history — the golden rule: **never rebase commits that others have already pulled.** Their history and yours diverge, and fixing that is painful.
- Conflicts are resolved per-commit, so you may hit the same conflict several times (`git rerere` helps).
- You lose the information that the work happened in parallel.

## Practical rules of thumb

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Cleaning up your own local branch before a PR | `git rebase -i main` |
| Pulling upstream changes into your unpushed feature branch | `git pull --rebase` |
| Landing a feature branch into a shared `main` | `git merge` (often `--no-ff`) |
| Anything already pushed and shared | `git merge` |

A common workflow: rebase locally to keep your feature branch tidy, then merge it into `main` so the merge commit records when the feature landed.

## Cleanup mechanics

If a rebase goes wrong, `git rebase --abort` returns you to the starting state; after it finished, `git reflog` still has the pre-rebase commits, so `git reset --hard HEAD@{n}` recovers them.

Also worth knowing: `git merge --squash` and squash-merge on GitHub collapse a branch into a single commit — linear history like rebase, but the individual commits vanish entirely.

Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history. Here's the same starting repo (`A` base, `B` on master, `C` on feature) taken both ways.

**Merge** — creates a new commit with two parents, preserving both lines:

```
$ git merge master
*   17774cb M: merge master into feature
|\
| * f820214 B: main work
* | abe104c C: feature work
|/
* 3172713 A: base
```

**Rebase** — replays your commits on top of the other branch, producing a straight line:

```
$ git rebase master
* 8481998 C: feature work
* 93ce516 B: main work
* 362092f A: base
```

Key differences:

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | branching graph, extra merge commit | linear, no merge commit |
| Existing commits | untouched | **rewritten** |
| Conflict resolution | once, in the merge commit | potentially once per replayed commit |
| Undo | `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` | same, but hashes already changed |

The rewrite is the part that matters. In the rebase demo, `C: feature work` had hash `e43d921` before and `8481998` after — same content, new commit object, because its parent changed:

```
--- feature commit hash BEFORE rebase ---
e43d921
--- feature commit hash AFTER rebase ---
8481998
```

That's why the rule of thumb is **don't rebase commits that others have pulled** — their history no longer matches yours, and pushing requires `--force-with-lease`.

Practical guidance:
- **Rebase** your local, unpushed feature branch onto the latest `main` to keep it current and get a clean linear history for review.
- **Merge** when integrating a finished branch into a shared branch, or any time the branch is public — the merge commit is an honest record of when integration happened.
- `git pull --rebase` avoids the noisy "Merge branch 'main' of origin..." commits from routine syncing.

So the explanation below is from the documented cache model, **unverified** on this machine — I couldn't run a build to produce receipts.

## The short answer

The build cache is a **chain, not a set**. Each instruction's cache key is derived from *the ID of the layer it's built on top of* plus the instruction itself. So a cache hit at step N requires a cache hit at every step before it.

Roughly:

```
key(step N) = hash( layerID(step N-1) , instruction text [, file checksums] )
```

Move an instruction and its parent changes, so its key changes, so it misses — and because it now produces a *different* layer ID, every instruction after it misses too. The instructions can be byte-identical and still all miss.

## Why "these two lines are independent" doesn't save you

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install -y curl      # A
RUN pip install requests         # B
```

Swapping A and B is semantically a no-op, but `B` now sits on the base image instead of on A's layer. Different parent → different key → miss, plus a cascade through everything below. Docker doesn't reason about whether two commands commute; it only hashes the chain.

## The case that actually bites people

```dockerfile
COPY . .                    # moved up
RUN npm ci                  # now rebuilds on every source edit
```

versus the intended order:

```dockerfile
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                  # only reruns when the manifests change
COPY . .
```

For `COPY`/`ADD`, the key also includes a checksum of the copied file contents. Hoisting a broad `COPY . .` above an expensive step means any touched file invalidates that step and all downstream ones. This is usually what people mean when they say reordering "busts the cache" — the reorder didn't just miss once, it moved a high-churn input in front of a slow step.

Same mechanic, less obvious sources:
- `ARG` — a changed build arg invalidates from its first *use* onward, so moving the `ARG` line moves where invalidation starts.
- `ENV`, `WORKDIR`, `USER` — cheap to run, but each still forms a link in the chain.

## BuildKit nuance

BuildKit builds a DAG rather than a strict line, so genuinely independent multi-stage branches don't invalidate each other, and it can skip stages nothing depends on. But *within* a linear run of instructions the parent-chain rule is unchanged — reordering still rewrites keys from the move point down.

## Practical rule

Order instructions from **least likely to change** to **most likely to change**: base image → system packages → dependency manifests → dependency install → application source. Anything expensive should sit above anything that churns.

Docker's layer cache is keyed on *history*, not on the individual line. That's the whole answer, and everything else follows from it.

## The cache key is a chain

For each instruction, the builder computes a cache key roughly as:

```
key(N) = hash( imageID(N-1) , instruction_text(N) )
```

`imageID(N-1)` is the result of everything above. So a cache hit at step N requires a hit at every step before it. The moment one step misses, its output ID changes, which changes the key of the next step, and so on to the bottom. Cache invalidation is a suffix, never a hole in the middle.

Reordering two lines changes what sits above each of them. Even though the instruction text is byte-identical, its parent ID is different, so the key is different, so it misses — and it takes every line below it down with it.

## Why this bites in practice

The classic:

```dockerfile
# fast
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .

# reordered — now every source edit re-runs npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
```

In the second version `RUN npm ci`'s parent is a layer containing your whole working tree. Touch any file, `COPY . .` misses (for `COPY`/`ADD` the key also folds in a checksum of the copied contents, not just the path text), and `npm ci` is forced to re-run.

The subtler ones:

- **Moving an `ARG` or `ENV` upward.** The build arg gets substituted into later instruction strings, so changing where it's declared — or changing its value — alters the text of every command that references it below.
- **Metadata instructions.** `LABEL`, `EXPOSE`, `WORKDIR`, `USER` produce no filesystem change but still occupy a slot in the chain. Sliding a `LABEL` from the bottom to the top shifts the parent ID of everything after it.
- **The build context.** `COPY . .` is only as stable as your `.dockerignore`. A new `node_modules/` or `.git` churn changes the checksum even if you touched no source.

## The heuristic this implies

Order lines by how often they change: base image, system packages, dependency manifests, dependency install, then application source last. You're not ordering for readability, you're ordering so the volatile stuff sits *below* the expensive stuff.

## Two BuildKit caveats

BuildKit builds a DAG rather than a strict line-by-line chain, so independent multi-stage branches don't invalidate each other — reordering across unrelated stages is often free. But *within* a stage the dependency chain is still linear, so the rule above holds.

And `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci` gives you a second line of defence: the layer still misses and the command still re-runs, but the package downloads come off a persistent cache mount, so the miss costs seconds rather than minutes.

## The cache is a chain, not a lookup table

Each instruction's cache key is a hash of **(parent layer ID + the instruction itself)** — and for `COPY`/`ADD`, plus a checksum of the copied file contents. So step N's key depends on the *resolved* key of step N-1.

That's the whole answer: reordering doesn't change what an instruction says, but it changes what its **parent** is. A `RUN npm ci` whose text is byte-identical hashes to a different key when the layer beneath it changed. First miss cascades to every step after it — Docker stops consulting the cache entirely once it misses one.

```dockerfile
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./     # A
RUN npm ci                # B, keyed on A's layer
COPY . .                  # C
```

Swap A and C and `npm ci` is now a child of "all your source" — so every source edit invalidates it. Same instruction, same text, different parent.

## Why it bites harder than people expect

- **`RUN` is cached on the literal string**, not on what it does. `RUN apt-get update` will happily reuse a six-month-old package index because the string didn't change. Conversely, changing a comment inside a `RUN` heredoc or adding whitespace *does* change the string and misses.
- **`ENV` and `ARG` leak into descendants.** `ARG` values get expanded into the cache keys of subsequent `RUN`s that reference them, so hoisting an `ARG` upward can silently bust the tail of the file.
- **`COPY . .` placed early** is the classic self-inflicted version — its checksum changes on any file touched, including the ones your build doesn't read. A `.dockerignore` is the fix, not reordering.
- **`WORKDIR`, `USER`, `LABEL`** look inert but are still layers with keys; moving them shifts everyone's parent.

BuildKit parallelizes across stages and does content-addressed keys, but *within* a stage the dependency chain is still linear — reordering still re-parents. `RUN --mount=type=cache` softens the pain (the npm/apt cache dir survives a miss, so you re-run but don't re-download) without preventing the miss.

## The rule that falls out

Order instructions **least-frequently-changing first**: base image → system packages → dependency manifests → dependency install → application source. Anything you move upward invalidates everything below it; anything you move downward is free.

Short answer: no, not as a default. `--force` on a shared branch overwrites the remote history unconditionally, so any commits a teammate pushed between your last fetch and your push are erased from the branch tip. Their local clones still have the old commits, so their next `git pull` either re-merges the deleted work back in or produces conflicts nobody expects.

When it's acceptable:

- **Your own topic/PR branch that only you push to** — routine after a rebase or amend.
- **A shared branch where everyone has agreed in advance** — a coordinated history rewrite (removing a leaked secret, `filter-repo` cleanup). Everyone needs to re-clone or hard-reset afterward.

What to use instead:

```
git push --force-with-lease
```

It refuses the push if the remote tip isn't what your last fetch recorded — so it fails instead of clobbering someone's new commits. Tighten it further with the explicit expected ref, which is safe even if a background `git fetch` refreshed your remote-tracking ref:

```
git push --force-with-lease=main:<sha-you-expect-remote-to-be-at>
```

For `main`/`master` or any branch with protection rules, the right answer is usually not forcing at all — use `git revert` to undo commits with new commits, which leaves everyone's history intact.

Short answer: no, not on a branch other people are working on.

**What actually happens.** `--force` sets the remote ref to your commit unconditionally. Any commits that were on the remote but aren't ancestors of yours become unreachable. Collaborators' next `git pull` on that branch either fails or, worse, "succeeds" by merging the old history back in — producing duplicated commits and conflicts. Anyone who had already pulled the old commits will silently reintroduce them.

**When it's fine:**
- Your own topic branch / PR branch that nobody else has checked out — cleaning up after a rebase or amend is the normal workflow.
- A shared branch where you've told everyone first and they're prepared to `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`.

**When it's not:**
- `main`, `master`, `develop`, release branches — these should have branch protection turned on so the question can't come up.
- Any branch where someone else may have pushed since you last fetched.

**Use `--force-with-lease` instead.** It refuses the push if the remote moved since your last fetch, so you can't clobber a teammate's commit you never saw:

```
git push --force-with-lease origin my-branch
```

One caveat: a background `git fetch` (some IDEs and shell prompts do this) updates your remote-tracking ref and makes the lease pass even though you never looked at the new commits. `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected-sha>` pins it explicitly, and newer git has `--force-if-includes` to tighten the default case.

**If a bad force-push already happened:** the old commits usually survive in the pusher's local reflog (`git reflog show origin/<branch>`) or in a collaborator's clone, so recovery is normally `git push --force origin <old-sha>:<branch>`.

Short answer: no, not safely — `--force` on a branch other people pull from is the classic way to destroy a colleague's commits.

**What actually goes wrong**

`git push --force` tells the remote "make this ref point at my commit, whatever is there now." If someone pushed between your last fetch and your push, their commits are no longer reachable from the branch tip. They still exist in the remote's reflog/object store for a while, but nobody sees them, and anyone who already pulled the old history gets a divergence they'll typically resolve by `git reset --hard origin/branch` — silently discarding the work.

**Use `--force-with-lease` instead**

```
git push --force-with-lease=refs/heads/main:<sha-you-expect>
```

or, more commonly, plain `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses the push if the remote ref moved since your last fetch. One trap worth knowing: a bare `--force-with-lease` compares against your remote-tracking ref, so if something ran `git fetch` in the background (an IDE, a `git pull --rebase` alias, a pre-push hook), the lease is refreshed and the safety check passes against history you never actually looked at. `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<sha>` with an explicit SHA closes that hole. Newer Git also has `--force-if-includes`, which additionally checks that the remote tip is an ancestor of something in your reflog.

**When force-pushing shared branches is fine**

- Your own feature branch that only you push to, even if others read it (rebasing before merge is normal).
- A PR branch, after telling reviewers — GitHub keeps review comments but they can go stale.
- Removing a leaked secret or oversized file, where rewriting history is the point. Coordinate: everyone re-clones or runs `git reset --hard`, and note that the secret is still compromised and must be rotated regardless.

**When it isn't**

- `main`/`master`/`develop`, or any branch CI and deploys track.
- Any branch where you can't reach everyone who has it checked out.

**Protection worth setting up**

Enable branch protection on the remote (GitHub: Settings → Branches → block force pushes; GitLab: protected branches). That's the real fix — it makes the question moot rather than relying on everyone remembering the right flag.

**If someone already force-pushed over work:** the commits are usually recoverable. Anyone who still has the old tip locally can find it with `git reflog` and push it back; on the server side, `git reflog` on the remote (or GitHub's Events API / a stale PR page showing the old SHA) can surface the lost commit before GC runs.

No — JSON object keys must be strings. Verified:

```
{1: "a"}     <- ERROR: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1
{"1": "a"}   <- OK
```

Details:

- **The grammar requires it.** RFC 8259 defines a member as `string : value`. An unquoted number in key position is a parse error, as above.
- **Quoted numbers are fine.** `{"1": "a"}` is valid — the key is the *string* `"1"`, not the number 1.
- **Serializers coerce silently.** `JSON.stringify({1: "a", 2.5: "b"})` produced `{"1":"a","2.5":"b"}` — numeric keys get stringified on the way out. Python's `json.dumps` does the same. So round-tripping `{1: "a"}` in JS/Python gives you back `{"1": "a"}`, and the key type changed. That's the usual source of bugs: `obj[1]` works in JS (it coerces on lookup too) but in Python `d[1]` raises `KeyError` after a round trip — you need `d["1"]`.

No — JSON object keys must be strings, always double-quoted. A bare number as a key is a syntax error:

```
$ python -c 'import json; json.loads("{1: \"a\"}")'
unquoted key -> JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)

$ node -e 'JSON.parse("{1:\"a\"}")'
unquoted key -> Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)
```

What you *can* do is quote the number — `{"1": "a"}` is valid JSON, and the key is the string `"1"`, not the integer 1:

```
python: {'1': 'a'}
node:   { '1': 'a' }
```

Two practical consequences:

- **Serializers coerce silently.** `json.dumps({1: 'a', True: 'b', None: 'c'})` produced `{"1": "b", "null": "c"}` — the integer `1` and boolean `True` both became the key `"1"`, so one entry was silently lost. JS does the same: `JSON.stringify({1:'a'})` → `{"1":"a"}`.
- **Round-tripping loses the type.** A Python dict keyed by ints comes back keyed by strings after a `dumps`/`loads` cycle. If you need integer keys preserved, use a list of `{"key": 1, "value": ...}` objects, or convert back explicitly on load.

No. In JSON, object keys must be double-quoted strings — the grammar allows nothing else.

```
'{1: 2}'   -> ERROR: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
'{"1": 2}' -> {'1': 2}
round-trip of python int key: {"1": 2}
type after load: ['str']
```

Points worth noting:

- `{"1": 2}` is valid, but the key is the **string** `"1"`, not the number 1.
- Languages that allow numeric keys (Python dicts, JS objects) silently stringify them on serialization — `json.dumps({1: 2})` emits `{"1": 2}`, and it comes back as `'1'`. Round-tripping `{1: 2}` does **not** give you back an int key.
- JS is the same: `JSON.stringify({1: 2})` → `'{"1":2}'`, and `Object.keys` on any object returns strings.
- Consequence: `{1: "a", "1": "b"}` collapses to one entry after a round trip through JSON. If you need integer keys preserved, use an array of `[key, value]` pairs or convert back explicitly on load.

No. It prevents one specific thing: two threads executing Python *bytecode* at the same time in one interpreter. Everything else is still parallel.

Measured just now on this machine (Python 3.13.5, 16 cores, 4 workers):

```
--- pure-Python CPU work ---
serial                               0.82s
ThreadPoolExecutor                   0.82s
ProcessPoolExecutor                  0.37s
  thread speedup 1.01x   process speedup 2.21x

--- hashlib (C ext, releases GIL) ---
serial                               0.49s
ThreadPoolExecutor                   0.12s
  thread speedup 3.93x

--- blocking I/O (time.sleep) ---
serial                               4.00s
ThreadPoolExecutor                   1.00s
  thread speedup 4.00x
```

What the three rows say:

**Threads do nothing for pure-Python CPU work** — 1.01x. This is the case people mean when they say "the GIL kills parallelism." Four threads adding integers in a loop take exactly as long as doing it one after the other.

**Threads give near-linear speedup the moment control leaves the interpreter.** `hashlib.sha256().update()` drops the GIL around the C hashing loop, so four threads hash concurrently: 3.93x. Same for numpy, zlib, image codecs, most DB drivers, and anything else whose hot loop is C. The GIL protects CPython's internal state (refcounts, dicts); code that isn't touching that state doesn't need to hold it.

**Blocking I/O is fully parallel** — 4.00x. Sockets, files, `sleep`, subprocess waits all release the GIL. Web scrapers and API fan-out get real concurrency from threads.

**And processes sidestep it entirely** — separate interpreters, separate GILs. The 2.21x rather than 4x is Windows `spawn` startup cost inside a 0.82s benchmark, not a parallelism ceiling; the work itself did run on four cores.

**PUT.** That's exactly what it's defined for: "store this representation at this URI." If the client already knows the URI, PUT is the verb that says so.

```http
PUT /orders/8a7f2c1e-...  HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: *
Content-Type: application/json

{ "item": "widget", "qty": 3 }

→ 201 Created        (first time)
→ 412 Precondition Failed   (already exists)
```

The reasons that actually matter:

**Idempotency.** A retried PUT lands in the same final state. This is the real payoff — a client generating a UUID and retrying through a flaky network can't accidentally create two orders. POST gives you no such guarantee, which is why POST-based creation needs a separate idempotency-key mechanism bolted on.

**`If-None-Match: *` gives you create-only semantics.** Without it, PUT will happily overwrite an existing resource. With it, the server returns 412 if the ID is taken. Pair with `If-Match: "<etag>"` for subsequent updates and you have a clean concurrency story with no extra vocabulary.

**Status codes:** 201 with a `Location` header on create, 200 or 204 on overwrite. Client-chosen ID that's malformed or violates a uniqueness rule → 422 or 409.

Where PUT stops being the right call:

- **Creation does more than store a resource.** If `POST /orders` charges a card, sends mail, or kicks off a workflow, PUT is lying — it claims the request is just a state assignment. Use POST.
- **The server must fill in fields.** PUT is full replacement; a client that can't send the complete representation shouldn't be using it. (PATCH for partial updates afterward.)
- **IDs live in a shared namespace where collisions are adversarial** (e.g. usernames). PUT works, but the 412-vs-403 distinction leaks who owns what. Sometimes POST with a server-side check is a cleaner boundary.

One common wrinkle: some frameworks and API gateways route PUT to an "update" handler by default and 404 on unknown IDs. That's a framework convention, not HTTP — you'll need to wire the create path explicitly.

Adding an optional parameter to a public function is backward-compatible — existing callers keep working unchanged — but it adds new functionality to the API surface. Per [semver.org](https://semver.org) item 7: "Minor version MUST be incremented if new functionality is added in a backward compatible manner."

Caveats where it becomes **major** instead:

- **Positional insertion** — if the parameter goes anywhere but last in a language with positional args, you've broken existing call sites.
- **Subclassing / interface implementation** — in languages where users implement your interface or override the method (Java, C#, TypeScript interfaces, Python ABCs), a changed signature breaks their implementations.
- **Function references** — callers passing your function as a callback with a strict arity/type signature may break (TypeScript, Rust trait bounds, C# delegates).
- **ABI-level languages** (C++, Rust with `#[no_mangle]`) — default arguments don't preserve ABI; the mangled symbol changes.

And it's never a patch: patch is reserved for backward-compatible bug fixes only, and a new parameter means consumers who depend on the new behavior need a version floor.

**Minor.**

Adding an optional parameter is a backward-compatible feature addition — existing callers compile and behave identically. Semver §7: "MINOR version when you add functionality in a backward compatible manner."

Three cases where it's actually **major**, worth checking before you tag:

1. **Inserted, not appended** — if the new param sits before existing ones in a language with positional args, every existing call shifts. Breaking.
2. **The function's signature is a contract others implement** — a TS interface method, an abstract/virtual method users override, a protocol. Widening the signature breaks implementers even though it doesn't break callers.
3. **The function is passed as a callback** where your library invokes it — same problem in reverse, if the extra arg changes arity expectations.

If it's appended, has a default, and nobody implements or overrides it: minor.

**Minor.** New backward-compatible functionality — existing callers keep working untouched.

It becomes **major** if any of these apply:

- **Positional insertion** — the parameter goes anywhere but the end of the signature, shifting existing positional args.
- **The function is overridden or implemented by users** — adding a param to an abstract method, interface member, or callback signature breaks their subclasses/implementations even though direct callers are fine.
- **The default changes existing behavior** — if omitting the parameter now yields different output than before, that's a breaking change dressed as an addition.
- **Signature is observable** — reflection, `inspect.signature`, arity checks (`fn.length` in JS), or `**kwargs` forwarding that validates against the signature.

It's only a **patch** if the parameter isn't actually reachable by users — e.g. the function is public in name but the whole module is documented as internal.

`EADDRINUSE` = "address already in use." Node asked the OS to bind a TCP port and the OS refused because something already holds it. Four usual causes:

1. **A previous run of your own server is still alive** — most common. Crashed terminal, nodemon that didn't reap the child, or a detached background process.
2. **Another app owns the port** — 3000/5000/8080 are crowded. On Windows, port 5000 is also grabbed by some system services, and Hyper-V/WSL reserve random port ranges (`netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp`).
3. **You call `listen()` twice** — e.g. `app.listen()` in a module that gets imported twice, or both an `http.createServer(app).listen()` and `app.listen()`.
4. **TIME_WAIT sockets** — rarer with Node since it sets `SO_REUSEADDR` by default, but shows up if you bind to the exact same local addr/port pair right after a hard close.

To find the culprit on Windows (replace 3000 with your port):

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress,OwningProcess
Get-Process -Id <OwningProcess>
```

Then `Stop-Process -Id <pid>` if it's your stale server.

## What EADDRINUSE means

`listen()` failed because the OS refused to bind the socket — some other socket already owns that `(address, port)` pair. Node surfaces it as an error event on the server, and if nothing handles it, the process crashes.

Four causes, roughly in order of how often they're the real one:

1. **A previous run of your own server is still alive.** Nodemon/ts-node-dev restarts, a detached `node index.js`, a terminal you closed without Ctrl-C. This is the common case.
2. **A different program owns the port.** 3000/5000/8080 are crowded — on Windows, port 5000 is a classic collision with services, and Hyper-V/WSL reserve blocks of ephemeral ports that will refuse binds with no visible listener.
3. **You call `listen()` twice in one process.** Usually an `app.listen()` in a module that gets imported by both your entrypoint and your test setup, or a hot-reload path re-running the bootstrap.
4. **`TIME_WAIT` on a recently-closed socket.** Only bites when you bind a specific address without `SO_REUSEADDR`; Node sets it by default on Linux/macOS, so this is rare there and more plausible on Windows with an explicit host bind.

## Finding which one it is

On Windows, this finds the owning process (replace 3000):

```powershell
netstat -ano | findstr :3000
# take the PID from the last column
tasklist /FI "PID eq <pid>"
```

Both integrate changes from one branch into another; merge preserves history as it happened, rebase rewrites it into a straight line.

**Merge** creates a new commit with two parents, joining the branches:

```
main:    A---B---C---M
                    /
feature:     D---E-/
```
Your feature commits keep their original hashes and parentage. History is truthful but has merge bubbles.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the target, making new commits with new hashes:

```
main:    A---B---C
feature:          D'---E'
```
Linear history, easier `git log`/`git bisect`, but D and E are different objects than before.

The practical rule: rebase your local, unpushed work onto updated `main` to avoid noise; merge when integrating into a shared branch. Never rebase commits others have already pulled — their history diverges from yours and the next `git pull` produces duplicates or conflicts.

Conflict handling also differs: merge stops once with all conflicts at once; rebase stops per replayed commit, so you may resolve the same conflict repeatedly (`git rerere` helps).

Practical differences:

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | true, branchy | linear, tidy |
| Commit hashes | preserved | rewritten |
| Conflicts | resolved once | possibly once per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | yes | no — force-push breaks collaborators |

Both integrate changes from one branch into another; merge preserves history as-is, rebase rewrites it.

**merge** creates a new commit with two parents, joining the branches. History shows exactly what happened, including the branch topology. Nothing already-committed changes hash.

**rebase** replays your commits one at a time onto the new base, producing new commits with new hashes. History comes out linear, as if you'd started from the latest upstream all along.

```
merge:                     rebase:
A---B---C  main            A---B---C  main
     \       \                      \
      D---E---M  feature              D'--E'  feature
```

Practical consequences:

- **Conflicts**: merge resolves once; rebase can make you resolve the same conflict per replayed commit (`git rerere` helps).
- **Shared branches**: never rebase commits others have pulled — their history diverges from yours and the next push needs `--force`. Rebase your own local work before it's pushed; merge anything public.
- **Bisect/blame**: linear rebased history is easier to bisect; merge history keeps the true context of when work was actually written.

Common workflow: `git pull --rebase` to keep your local feature branch current, then a real merge (often `--no-ff`) when it lands on main.

Another process already holds the port your server binds to — `listen()` fails because the address/port pair is taken.

Common sources: a previous run of your own server that didn't exit (nodemon restart, orphaned `node` process), a second `listen()` call on the same port in your code, or an unrelated service on that port.

Find the holder (Windows, replace 3000):

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen | Select-Object OwningProcess |
  ForEach-Object { Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess }
```

Then `Stop-Process -Id <pid>`, or change the port.

